chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
title: Tuba player Barney Aquilino, the six-day bicycle race and Vincent Lopez
summary: He tells how a charity bicycle-race job led to Vincent Lopez's management, his $75 weekly contract and recording fees, and theatergoing in New York.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I had a tuba player, Barney Aquilino. He was with James Barney. I got him afterwards in New York. And he was more or less my promoter. He got me in the middle of a dance hall. I wore up in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. There was two dance halls, big ball, beautiful big ball. They were fighting each other. And I happened to play at the six day bicycle races. You see I lived a long life, and I'll tell you a long, I mean a musical life. I'm playing at the six day bicycle races for the benefit of poor children. And in the box there there's Vincent Lopez and God knows who, all the big mansees and all. They offer a hundred dollars for a sprint. Well if I say, who wins that sprint, it gets a hundred bucks. And the sprint's all night. So they asked me to play. I said certainly for poor children. I go there with my band. They don't have a piano. Well we've got to play. So I played It Had To Be You. And they had an arrangement in stop time where I took all the breaks. The band goes, It had to be you. And I come in, all over the joint. You know like that way. Crap. But good. You know. They're all up there, who is this guy? So they said, no, Johnny D. Dre from the Halls, I play another tune. Every prize fighter and bum from the Halls that was in New York was on my bandstand looking for a handout. And I'm playing for nothing in the joint, see. But the next morning, my phone rings incessantly. I'm off and jump. Everybody wants to be my agent. Everybody wants to be my agent. So I signed up with Vincent Lopez. And he appointed Mrs. Marvin Fuller, Mrs. Earl Fuller as my manager. You never heard of Earl Fuller? Carman Blair? No. Band leader from the Pacific Coast. When he made his entrance to New York, he was on special train. He recorded for Victor, didn't he? I think he did. I don't know. But anyhow, his wife, he died and his wife became an agent. And she sends me to Harrisburg. She goes to Oakland to You know what I mean? In those days. So I paid the boys' hotel booth. I could have stuck it in my pocket. They didn't know what I was getting. Because I had them on the contract for $75 a week. And $25 for each recording. That's all they got for the recording. But I got a lump sum on it. $50 and 2% royalties. So Vincent Lopez is the only one who sent me a while when I opened this to Burbank. I put it in my scrapbook. I wish you had success in a long engagement. I mean he's a man that does things. He's getting old now. He still plays Nola and all that. Last time I saw him he didn't know I was in the place. I didn't want to impose myself on him. I think they have to entertain him. And my wife and I only had two weeks. We saw 13 shows in 11 days. And I'd get the tickets. Don't think I didn't. See Ray Bowles is a personal friend of mine. I played golf with Ray in his show. He was being featured. I'm talking about this a long time ago. And then for Oklahoma and Carousel and all I'd go up and give the... After everybody was seated inside the show I'd talk to the man at the box office and I'd say, this is my card. I'm an auctioneer from New Orleans. I'm on a bus and it's holiday. And if you've got two seats any day, any matinee, I'll take it. And I always got seats without pants. I saw the original version of Show Boop, Charlie Whittaker. I knew Charlie Whittaker. He was married to Blanche Franey. You ever heard of Blanche Franey?
